title: Convolution as a sliding dot product

items.prose: A 4 by 4 image $\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ meets the kernel $\mathbf{K} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, slid with no flip over valid positions. Rows and columns count from 0.

parts.question: What is $Y_{00}$, the output for the top-left window?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pair each pixel of the window with the weight in the same place.

byKey.flipped: You reversed the kernel in both directions. The slide keeps it as written.
byKey.matmul: You added up the matrix product of the window and the kernel. Multiply matching entries instead.

parts.question: Using $Y_{00} = 5$ from part 1, what is the sum of the whole first row $Y_{00} + Y_{01} + Y_{02}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide the window right one column at a time.

byKey.first-only: That is only $Y_{00}$. The row has three outputs.

parts.question: The loss sends back $\partial L/\partial Y_{ij} = 1$ on the first row of outputs and 0 elsewhere. What is $\partial L / \partial K_{11}$?

feedback.correct: $K_{11}$ meets $X_{1, j+1}$ along the first row of windows: $3 + 1 + 0 = 4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which pixel does $K_{11}$ meet in each of the three windows?

byKey.corner: That adds $X_{00} + X_{01} + X_{02}$, the pixels $K_{00}$ meets.
byKey.all: That is the row of outputs again. The gradient adds pixels, not outputs.

parts.question: Using $\partial L / \partial K_{11} = 4$ from part 3, one gradient step with learning rate 0.1 moves $K_{11}$ from 2 to what? Give a decimal to 1 place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Step against the gradient.

byKey.up: You stepped with the gradient. Descent subtracts it.
byKey.no-rate: You subtracted the whole gradient. Multiply it by 0.1 first.

items.prose: Eight closes in £: $100, 102, 101, 104, 103, 105, 107, 106$. A weighted mean uses the kernel $(0.25, 0.25, 0.5)$, oldest weight first, slid with no flip.

parts.question: How many valid outputs are there?

byKey.all: One per close counts windows that are not full.

parts.question: Of the 6 outputs from part 1, numbered from 0, what is $y_1$? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The window of $y_1$ starts at the second close.

byKey.flipped: You put 0.5 on the oldest close of the window. It belongs on the newest, 104.

parts.question: pandas would write the $y_1 = 102.75$ of part 2 on its window’s last row. Counting rows from 0, which row is that?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Output $t$ covers rows $t$ to $t + 2$.

byKey.start: That is the window’s first row.

explain.text: Output $t$ sits on row $t + k - 1$: row 3, the close of 104.

parts.question: Instead of the 6 valid outputs of part 1, a "same" output pads with one zero before the first close. What is the first output then? Give a whole number of pounds.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The first padded window is $(0, 100, 102)$.

byKey.edge: The border was filled by copying the nearest pixel, 100 (edge padding). Zero padding would write a 0 instead.
byKey.half: You kept only the newest close, $0.5 \times 102$. The 100 still gets its 0.25.

explain.text: The padded window $(0, 100, 102)$ gives 76, far below every close: zero padding invents a crash at the start.

items.prose: A kernel $\mathbf{k} = (1, 1)$ slides with no flip over the signal $(1, 0, 2, 1)$; the target is $(0.5, 1, 2)$ and the loss is the mean of the squared errors.

parts.question: What is the loss? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Outputs first, then errors, then the mean square.

byKey.sum: That is the sum of squares. The loss is their mean.
byKey.no-square: You averaged the errors without squaring them.

parts.question: Using the errors $(0.5, 1, 1)$ from part 1, what is $\partial L/\partial k_0$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

byKey.k1: That is $\partial L/\partial k_1$, which meets $x_1, x_2, x_3$.

parts.question: With $\partial L/\partial k_0 = 1.6667$ from part 2 and $\partial L/\partial k_1 = 2$, take one step at learning rate 0.1. What is the new $k_0$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the rate times the gradient.

parts.question: With the new kernel $(0.8333, 0.8)$ from part 3, what is the loss now? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Recompute the three outputs with the new weights.

byKey.old: That is the loss before the step.
byKey.sum: That is the sum of the squared errors; take the mean.

explain.text: Outputs $(0.8333, 1.6, 2.4667)$ less the target give errors $(0.3333, 0.6000, 0.4667)$. Their mean square is 0.230, down from 0.75.
